what_it_does: Before a chip design is sent to the factory, engineers run logic synthesis — a process that converts a high-level circuit description into an optimized network of basic logic gates. One important step is refactoring, where the tool picks a small window (called a cut) of nearby gates, finds a mathematically equivalent but smaller or faster implementation, and swaps it in. The problem is that 98% of these candidate cuts turn out not to improve anything, so the tool wastes almost all its time evaluating dead ends. ELF trains a machine-learning classifier on historical synthesis runs to predict, before the expensive resynthesis step, whether a given cut is likely to yield an improvement. Cuts predicted to be unpromising are skipped entirely. This is plugged into the widely used ABC logic synthesis tool's refactor operator, and the claimed result is substantially faster synthesis with little or no quality loss, though exact numbers would require the full paper.
